title: Biomass-to-hard carbon for sodium-ion batteries: synthesis strategies, sodium storage mechanisms, and structure–performance relationships
content: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) have emerged as a promising alternative to lithium-ion batteries for large-scale energy storage applications due to the natural abundance, low cost, and wide geographical distribution of sodium resources. However, the development of high-performance anode materials remains a major challenge because conventional graphite exhibits limited sodium-storage capability, resulting from the large ionic radius of Na+. Among the various anode candidates, biomass-derived hard carbon (BHC) has attracted significant attention owing to its sustainable origin, tunable microstructure, environmental compatibility, and favorable electrochemical properties. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in BHC anodes for SIBs, with particular emphasis on synthesis strategies, precursor engineering, structural characteristics, sodium-storage mechanisms, and electrochemical performance relationships. Different preparation approaches, including direct pyrolysis, activation methods, heteroatom doping, surface engineering, and multi-step carbonization, are critically discussed in relation to their influence on interlayer spacing, porosity, defect density, graphitization degree, and solid electrolyte interphase formation. The role of diverse biomass precursors such as agricultural residues, lignocellulosic materials, algae, and biopolymers is also analyzed to establish structure–property correlations. Furthermore, the review highlights the sodium-storage mechanisms in BHC, including adsorption, intercalation, and pore-filling processes, together with the effects of pore architecture and heteroatom functionalities on ion transport and storage behavior. Current limitations, including low initial coulombic efficiency, structural heterogeneity, ash-related impurities, and scalability challenges, are systematically evaluated alongside recent optimization strategies involving nano-engineering, composite formation, and interface regulation. Overall, biomass-derived hard carbon represents a sustainable and technically viable anode material for next-generation sodium-ion batteries, although further advances in precursor standardization, mechanistic understanding, and scalable manufacturing are required to accelerate practical commercialization.
